chief_complaint: severe RUQ pain, fever, and positive Murphy sign
hpi_details: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with 2 days of severe, constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to his right shoulder blade, along with fever, nausea, and vomiting, especially worse after fatty meals.
ideas: He thinks he has severe acid reflux or terrible indigestion from eating greasy takeout over the weekend.
concerns: He is worried that the pain spreading to his shoulder blade is a warning sign of an early heart attack like his father had.
expectations: He hopes to get prescription-strength antacids and anti-nausea medicine so he can keep food down and go back to work.

investigation_events.title: Urgent acute cholecystitis results
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent acute cholecystitis results are now available; IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.value: Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, pericholecystic fluid, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 5 mm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Cholecystitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes NPO status, IV fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission when feasible, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe RUQ pain, fever, and positive Murphy sign

Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with 2 days of severe, constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to his right shoulder blade, along with fever, nausea, and vomiting, especially worse after fatty meals.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 108, BP 124/78. RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation); no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Labs: mild leukocytosis with left shift and mildly elevated LFTs. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), and pericholecystic fluid, consistent with acute cholecystitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Cholecystitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: High fever with rigors — suggests gangrenous cholecystitis.
management_principles: Keep the patient NPO, provide IV fluids, and start IV antibiotics with gram-negative and anaerobic coverage
Obtain RUQ ultrasound and consult surgery for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy
Counsel the patient on the diagnosis and the need for surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 23-year-old male presents with 2 days of severe, constant right upper quadrant pain radiating to his right shoulder blade, along with fever, nausea, and vomiting, especially worse after fatty meals.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.6C, HR 108, BP 124/78. RUQ tenderness with a positive Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpation); no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Labs: mild leukocytosis with left shift and mildly elevated LFTs. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), and pericholecystic fluid, consistent with acute cholecystitis.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, provide IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and obtain right-upper-quadrant ultrasound and relevant laboratory tests. Start empiric IV antibiotics with appropriate gram-negative and anaerobic coverage according to local guidance (for example, ceftriaxone plus metronidazole when suitable). Obtain early surgical consultation for laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the index admission when feasible.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Cholecystitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Cholecystitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: NPO, IV fluids, IV Cefazolin, laparoscopic cholecystectomy

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone obstructs the cystic duct, causing gallbladder inflammation with persistent RUQ pain, fever, and a positive Murphy's sign.
red_flags: High fever with rigors — suggests gangrenous cholecystitis

must_ask.say: Where is the pain, and does it radiate to your back or shoulder?
Did this start after a fatty meal?
Has the pain been constant rather than coming and going?

The pain is right under my ribs on the upper right side, and it has stayed in that exact spot without shifting anywhere else.
Yes, the pain shoots through to my back and right shoulder blade.
It is a steady, severe, aching pain that never completely lets up.
I would rate it an 8 out of 10 right now, and it has stayed intense since yesterday.
It gets noticeably worse whenever I try to eat, especially greasy food, and nothing I do seems to relieve it.
The pain has been constant without stopping for the past two days.
No, I've never had belly pain like this before.
I have felt very nauseated and vomited three times, mostly yellowish fluid and whatever I ate.
I haven't had diarrhea, my bowels moved normally yesterday, and I'm still passing gas without any blood in the stool.
Yes, I've had a fever since yesterday and felt feverish and shaky with chills.
No, my skin and eyes look normal, and my urine and stool colors haven't changed.
No pain when I urinate, no burning, and no blood in my urine.
No, I have not felt lightheaded or passed out.
No chest pain, pressure, or shortness of breath, except that breathing deeply hurts my upper belly.
About two days ago before this started, I ate fried chicken for dinner, but I didn't drink any alcohol.
I took some ibuprofen yesterday to try to ease the pain, but it didn't help at all.
No, I don't have any irregular heart rhythm, blood clots, or vascular problems.
I figured it was just really bad heartburn or indigestion from eating greasy takeout food.
My dad had a heart attack in his forties, so I'm scared this pain spreading into my shoulder might be my heart giving out.
I'm hoping for some strong prescription antacids and nausea pills so I can stop throwing up and get back to work.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries or needed to stay in a hospital before.
I am not taking any regular prescription medicines or herbal supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
No, I have never smoked in my life.
I drink occasionally when hanging out with friends, maybe one or two beers a month.
I am a 23-year-old college student living alone in an off-campus apartment.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, heart rate is 108 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, body temperature is 38.6°C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
Anicteric sclerae bilaterally and pink conjunctivae without pallor.
Clear breath sounds heard bilaterally without crackles or wheezing.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no distension, visible pulsations, or surgical scars.
Normoactive bowel sounds present in all four quadrants.
Severe tenderness on palpation localized to the right upper quadrant; abdomen is soft without involuntary guarding or diffuse rigidity.
Positive Murphy's sign with sudden arrest of inspiration during deep palpation of the right upper quadrant.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any quadrant.
No tenderness at McBurney's point, and negative psoas and obturator signs.
Normal sphincter tone, no mucosal masses or tenderness, and no gross blood on the examining glove.
